title: The queue that should not exist
subtitle: I built an inference queue manager with two-stage backpressure and permit-carrying requests, then found the runtime already had a token-based queue, and reduced mine to a wrapper
technologies: Capacity engineering, backpressure and load testing

stats.label: requests in flight at most, bounded by a channel
lines in the wrapper that remains
lines in the token queue it almost duplicated

lede: Between the services that need text generated and the engine that generates it, I built a queue manager. It was a good one. Then I read the runtime underneath it properly. The saturated inference runtime already had a token-capacity queue: a lock-free multi-producer queue that reserved token budget with an atomic compare-and-swap, drained up to the engine's batch token limit, and returned a typed backpressure error when full. It did at the token level, where the engine actually has limits, what my manager did at the request level.
quote: Two layers of backpressure with different units would have fought each other, and the request-level one would have won by starving the token-level one of work.
evidence: Backpressure design: a request-level queue with permit-carrying requests, at most 64 in flight and the permit released on every path, built and then reduced to a wrapper.
Inference serving architecture: the runtime's lock-free token-capacity queue recognised as doing admission where the engine has its limits, and admission delegated to it.
Software architecture simplification: a second backpressure layer in different units removed before it could starve the token queue; the wrapper is about 1,200 lines and the queue 1,600.
author: Corey James
